rich_summary: This section continues the description of sacred pilgrimage sites (tirthas) recounted to Yudhishthira, emphasizing regions associated with ancient sacrifices, sages, and rivers such as Saraswati and Drisadwati. The narrative highlights holy places like Gangadwara and the hermitage of Badrinath (Vadari), portrayed as the dwelling of Narayana, where gods and rishis gather and where the divine presence makes the entire universe’s sanctity converge. The passage stresses that visiting these places with ascetics brings spiritual merit and relief from anxiety. The scene then shifts: the sage Lomasa arrives and reports news from heaven. He has seen Arjuna seated beside Indra, having gained powerful celestial weapons—including the Brahma‑sira—and mastery of arts. Indra’s message urges Yudhishthira to practice austerities while awaiting Arjuna’s return, foreshadowing future conflicts with mighty warriors like Karna.

highlight_spans.why: Introduces the sacred geography and ritual generosity associated with Sahadeva and ancient sacrifices.
Describes revered sages and ritual sites, reinforcing the theme of pilgrimage and accumulated spiritual merit.
The theological climax describing Narayana/Vishnu at Vadari as the cosmic center where all sacredness converges.
The dramatic arrival of the sage Lomasa and the gathering around him, signaling a narrative shift from geography to news of Arjuna.
Reveals that Arjuna has gained the devastating Brahma‑sira weapon and other celestial arms, a pivotal development for the epic’s future battles.

top_scenes.scene_text: At Badrinath, gods and radiant rishis gather on golden riverbanks of the Ganga to worship the luminous Narayana amid snowy Himalayan peaks.
The sage Lomasa arrives before Yudhishthira and the Pandavas seated among Brahmanas in the forest, all gathered around him like gods around Indra.
In Indra’s celestial court, Arjuna sits beside the king of the gods, surrounded by divine weapons and astonished sages.
